issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, the trigger 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile clinically unless there is additional trauma content involving female perpetrators or a separate interpersonal trauma; nothing else in the profile supports that specific gendered trigger.

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: 'When people say things like my ex' implies a salient intimate-relationship trauma context that is not reflected anywhere else in the threat, memory, appraisal, or strategy items, making it a poor fit with the stated index trauma of terrorism.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after terrorism, but phrasing the event as happening 'because of the way I acted' suggests a strong personal-causation formulation. With the rest of the profile centered on external danger, startle, flashbacks, and monitoring others, this specific appraisal is insufficiently supported and sits awkwardly with the terrorism trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger item about 'my ex' is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of terrorism and the rest of the profile. It implies an intimate-relationship trauma context rather than reminders of a terrorist event, whereas the other trigger items (old photos, alcohol smell) and threat items are trauma-related.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the terrorism trauma context as presented here. In the absence of any terrorism-specific circumstance suggesting personal responsibility, 'The event happened because of the way I acted' implies causal responsibility for the attack, which is clinically implausible for this patient profile and not supported by the other selected items.

vignette:
When the bomb went off at the outdoor market in downtown Oakland, Srey was buying lemongrass. She remembers the exact shade of green in the bundle she was holding, the way the rubber band cut into her thumb, and then the sound-not a bang so much as a pressure that folded the air inward. She was thrown sideways into a metal cart stacked with mangoes. Her left eardrum perforated immediately, and for the first few seconds she existed in a muffled, ringing world where the dust looked like fog and the screaming came from very far away. The smell that stayed with her, the one she cannot shake, was not smoke or blood but the sharp, sweet reek of alcohol-based hand sanitizer that had exploded from a vendor's stall. That smell, even now, eight years later, can drop her back into the concrete and the ringing before she has time to brace herself.

Srey is fifty-seven, a married interior designer who works from a home studio in a quiet suburb. She has built a career on creating calm, orderly spaces, and she used to pride herself on her ability to walk into a client's chaotic renovation and see exactly what needed to happen. That confidence has eroded slowly, then all at once. She finds herself unable to tolerate even small disruptions now-a misplaced paint swatch, a contractor who is ten minutes late-and she has come to believe that she simply cannot cope with the slightest upset. The world, she is certain, is a dangerous place, and she has to be on guard all the time. She watches people closely, scanning their hands, their expressions, the way they move through a room. When a client reaches out to touch her arm to make a point, she flinches so hard she knocks over her coffee. She has started doing the initial consultations by video call, and she avoids showing clients the finished spaces in person. The consequence is that she has lost three major contracts in the last year. Her husband, who is patient and bewildered, has taken over the grocery shopping because she cannot walk into a store without the alcohol smell from the cleaning aisle triggering a visceral, full-body re-experiencing of the market. She feels, sometimes, as though she is back there, as though the present is a thin film over something much more real.

To manage the unbearable pressure that builds in her chest, Srey has developed strategies that she knows are not healthy but that feel necessary. She hurts herself physically-digging her nails into her forearms, pressing the heel of her hand into her thigh-because the sharp, clean pain cuts through the fog and gives her a few minutes of quiet. She runs, sometimes for two hours at a time, until her knees ache and her lungs burn, because exhaustion is the only thing that reliably dims the hypervigilance. And she eats, more than she means to, late at night when the memories press in: crackers, bread, anything that requires chewing and swallowing and occupies her hands and mouth so she does not have to think. The weight gain has been gradual, but it is another thing she monitors, another reason to feel that she is losing control.

What finally brought Srey to seek help was a moment that terrified her more than the bomb itself. Last month, her daughter sent her a photo from a family vacation years before the attack-Srey at a picnic, laughing, her hair loose. Srey looked at the photo and felt nothing. The woman in the picture was a stranger. She could not connect to that version of herself, could not remember what it felt like to be unguarded. That night, she sat on the floor of her studio and hurt herself more seriously than she ever had, and in the morning she called a therapist. She is afraid of what she might do if she keeps going this way. She is also afraid that talking about the event will make it worse, that the memories will become even more real. But she is more afraid of the alternative: a life in which she is a stranger to everyone she loves, watching the world from behind glass, waiting for the next explosion.
